summary.text: Take \(p=13\): the relevant Legendre symbols are \((3/13)=1\) and \((2/13)=(5/13)=-1\), while \(13=3\cdot1^2+10\cdot1^2\), and every such representation forces \(x^2=1\). Since \((-1/13)=1\), the asserted congruence would give \(S(13)\equiv14\pmod{169}\), but direct evaluation of the finite sum gives \(S(13)\equiv138\pmod{169}\).

full_proof.text:
We disprove the conjecture by using the prime \(p=13\), for which clause (3) gives an incorrect residue.

Recall that
\[
T_k(b,c)=[X^k](X^2+bX+c)^k
 =\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}
 \binom{k}{i}\binom{k-i}{i}b^{k-2i}c^i,
\]
and
\[
S(p)=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\binom{2k}{k}T_k(2,81)T_k(14,81).
\]

First, \(13\) is prime and \(13>7\). The nonzero quadratic residues modulo \(13\) are
\[
1^2,2^2,3^2,4^2,5^2,6^2\equiv 1,4,9,3,12,10\pmod {13},
\]
so their set is
\[
\{1,3,4,9,10,12\}.
\]
Consequently
\[
\left(\frac{3}{13}\right)=1,
\qquad
\left(\frac{2}{13}\right)=-1,
\qquad
\left(\frac{5}{13}\right)=-1,
\qquad
\left(\frac{-1}{13}\right)=1.
\]
Thus the quadratic-character assumptions in clause (3) hold. In the notation of the OEIS statement, which writes two of these symbols as \((p/3)\) and \((p/5)\), the same hypotheses also hold directly:
\[
\left(\frac{13}{3}\right)=\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)=1,
\qquad
\left(\frac{13}{5}\right)=\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)=-1,
\]
while \((2/13)=-1\) as above.

The required quadratic-form representation exists, since
\[
13=3\cdot 1^2+10\cdot 1^2.
\]
Moreover, every integral representation
\[
13=3x^2+10y^2
\tag{1}
\]
has \(x^2=1\). Indeed, both terms on the right of (1) are nonnegative. Hence \(10y^2\le 13\), so \(y^2\) is either \(0\) or \(1\). It cannot be \(0\), because then (1) would say \(3x^2=13\). Therefore \(y^2=1\), and (1) reduces to
\[
3x^2=13-10=3,
\]
so \(x^2=1\). This observation also shows that allowing the conclusion to choose any representation of \(13\), rather than requiring it to use the initially exhibited representation, cannot change the predicted residue.

We now compute \(S(13)\) modulo \(13^2=169\). The following table lists, for each \(0\le k\le 12\), the residues modulo \(169\) of the central binomial coefficient, the two generalized central trinomial coefficients, the resulting summand, and the cumulative sum. Every entry is obtained by substituting in the finite formula for \(T_k\) displayed above and reducing modulo \(169\).

\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r|r|r|r}
k&\binom{2k}{k}&T_k(2,81)&T_k(14,81)&
\binom{2k}{k}T_k(2,81)T_k(14,81)&\text{cumulative sum}\\ \hline
0&  1&  1&  1&  1&  1\\
1&  2&  2& 14& 56& 57\\
2&  6&166& 20&147& 35\\
3& 20&135& 84&  2& 37\\
4& 70&  6& 91& 26& 63\\
5& 83& 38& 45&139& 33\\
6& 79&162&102& 40& 73\\
7& 52&112&129& 91&164\\
8& 26&150& 65&  0&164\\
9&117& 14& 22& 39& 34\\
10&39& 23&164& 78&112\\
11&26&166& 45& 39&151\\
12&156&116&142&156&138
\end{array}
\qquad (\bmod 169).
\]

For clarity, this table can also be reproduced recursively from the elementary coefficient identity
\[
nT_n(b,c)=b(2n-1)T_{n-1}(b,c)
 -(b^2-4c)(n-1)T_{n-2}(b,c),
\]
with \(T_0(b,c)=1\) and \(T_1(b,c)=b\). For \(1\le n\le12\), \(n\) is invertible modulo \(169\), so this recurrence uniquely gives the displayed residues. As a sample direct check, at \(k=2\),
\[
T_2(b,c)=b^2+2c,
\]
whence
\[
T_2(2,81)=4+162=166,
\qquad
T_2(14,81)=196+162=358\equiv20\pmod{169}.
\]
The corresponding summand is
\[
\binom42\,166\cdot20=6\cdot166\cdot20\equiv147\pmod{169},
\]
as in the table.

The last cumulative entry gives
\[
S(13)\equiv138\pmod{169}.
\tag{2}
\]

Clause (3), on the other hand, predicts for every applicable representation that
\[
S(13)\equiv
\left(\frac{-1}{13}\right)\bigl(2\cdot13-12x^2\bigr)
\pmod{169}.
\]
We have already shown that \((-1/13)=1\) and that every representation (1) has \(x^2=1\). Therefore the conjectured right-hand side is
\[
1\cdot(26-12)=14\pmod{169}.
\tag{3}
\]
But \(138\not\equiv14\pmod{169}\), since their difference is \(124\), which is not divisible by \(169\). Equations (2) and (3) contradict the conclusion of clause (3) at the prime \(p=13\). Hence Conjecture 3 for OEIS A336982 is false.
